# Broken cipher DES, 3DES or RC4, or an insecure TLS cipher suite (Go)

`qualor:go/weak-cipher` · Issue · Severity: Medium · [CWE-327](https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/327.html) · OWASP Top 10: [A04:2025 Cryptographic Failures](https://top10.owasp.org/2025/A04_2025-Cryptographic_Failures/), [A02:2021 Cryptographic Failures](https://top10.owasp.org/2021/A02_2021-Cryptographic_Failures/)

## What it finds

<!-- begin: what-it-finds -->
Use of the broken ciphers DES, Triple DES and RC4 from the Go standard library:
`des.NewCipher`, `des.NewTripleDESCipher` and `rc4.NewCipher`, also when the package is imported
under another name.

It also finds TLS cipher suites that `crypto/tls` lists in `InsecureCipherSuites` (RC4, 3DES, RSA
key exchange, and CBC with SHA-256) enabled in the `CipherSuites` of a `tls.Config`: in the
literal, assigned to the field, or in a list variable used there.
<!-- end: what-it-finds -->

## Why it matters

<!-- begin: why-it-matters -->
The Go documentation calls these ciphers "cryptographically broken and should not be used for
secure applications". DES keys are short enough to search, Triple DES has a 64-bit block that
leaks data over long sessions, and RC4's key stream is biased. Data encrypted with them can be
recovered, and because none of them authenticates the data, it can also be changed unnoticed.
<!-- end: why-it-matters -->

## Example

<!-- begin: example -->
**Noncompliant:** a token is encrypted with Triple DES.

```go
package vault

import "crypto/des"

func Encrypt(key, block []byte) ([]byte, error) {
	c, err := des.NewTripleDESCipher(key)
	if err != nil {
		return nil, err
	}
	out := make([]byte, len(block))
	c.Encrypt(out, block)
	return out, nil
}
```

**Compliant:** AES-GCM, an authenticated cipher.

```go
package vault

import (
	"crypto/aes"
	"crypto/cipher"
	"crypto/rand"
)

func Encrypt(key, plaintext []byte) ([]byte, error) {
	block, err := aes.NewCipher(key)
	if err != nil {
		return nil, err
	}
	gcm, err := cipher.NewGCM(block)
	if err != nil {
		return nil, err
	}
	nonce := make([]byte, gcm.NonceSize())
	if _, err := rand.Read(nonce); err != nil {
		return nil, err
	}
	return gcm.Seal(nonce, nonce, plaintext, nil), nil
}
```
<!-- end: example -->

## How to fix

<!-- begin: how-to-fix -->
- Use an authenticated cipher: AES-GCM (`aes.NewCipher` with `cipher.NewGCM`) or
  ChaCha20-Poly1305 (`golang.org/x/crypto/chacha20poly1305`).
- Use a fresh random nonce for every message, and store it with the ciphertext.
- In a `tls.Config`, leave `CipherSuites` unset (Go's default list) or name only suites that
  `tls.CipherSuites()` returns, such as `tls.TLS_ECDHE_ECDSA_WITH_AES_128_GCM_SHA256`.
- Data already encrypted with DES, 3DES or RC4 should be decrypted once and encrypted again with
  the new cipher.
<!-- end: how-to-fix -->

## Frameworks and APIs covered

- `crypto/des`
- `crypto/rc4`
- `crypto/tls`

## Known limits

<!-- begin: known-limits -->
- Cipher suites written as numbers (`0x0005`), lists filled in a loop (from
  `tls.InsecureCipherSuites()`, say), and lists passed through functions or your own struct
  fields before they reach a `tls.Config` are not reported.
- A local variable that shadows the package name (`des := ...; des.NewCipher(k)`), or another
  package with the same last path element imported under an alias next to `crypto/des` or
  `crypto/rc4`, is taken for the cipher package.
<!-- end: known-limits -->

## Tests

The test file [`rules/go/crypto/weak-cipher.go`](../../../rules/go/crypto/weak-cipher.go) holds every case the rule reports or accepts:
lines marked `ruleid:` must be reported and lines marked `ok:` must not. The known limits are
marked `todoruleid:` (missed) and `todook:` (wrongly reported). `npm test` runs them with OpenGrep,
and checks the example above as well.
